entries.name: Apple
entries.spread: from the Silk Road west to Europe, east into China 2,000+ years ago; Americas after 1492
entries.notes: The world's most planted temperate fruit; more than 7,500 cultivars. Orchards and cider apples are the iconic variety.

entries.name: Banana (dessert)
entries.spread: from New Guinea through SE Asia and India; plantains to Africa; global tropics by the 19th century
entries.notes: A giant herb, not a tree; Cavendish dominates world trade. Cut by hurricane in exposed sites.

entries.name: Grape (wine and table)
entries.spread: Mesopotamia, Phoenicia, Greece and Rome; Americas after 1492
entries.notes: The founding fruit of wine; early evidence is wine residue in Georgian clay jars (qvevri) ~6000 BCE.

entries.name: Sweet orange
entries.spread: China and India to Arabia; sweet orange reached Europe by the 15th century with Portuguese navigators; Americas after 1492
entries.notes: All sweet oranges descend from a few Chinese ancestors; an ancient pomelo x mandarin hybrid.

entries.name: Mango
entries.spread: India and SE Asia; East Africa; Americas with the Portuguese in the 16th century
entries.notes: The 'king of fruits'; sacred in Hindu tradition. Huge old trees can live for centuries.

entries.name: Pear (European)

domesticated.where: Europe and the Caucasus (European pear; Asian Pyrus pyrifolia separately in China)

entries.spread: Europe and W Asia since antiquity; Americas after 1600; Asian pear across E and S Asia
entries.notes: Often planted where apples struggle; fire blight is the great enemy.

entries.name: Peach
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Chinese peach relatives (Prunus mira / P. kansuensis)
entries.spread: China, by ~300 BCE in Greece, then Rome; Americas after 1500; China still grows over 60% of world production
needs: winter chilling (low-chill cultivars for the subtropics)
entries.notes: Domesticated in the Yangtze delta as early as ~6000 BCE; the species is likely a cultigen, with no true wild form.

entries.name: Plum (European)
entries.spread: Europe and W Asia since antiquity; Japanese plum to Asia and global; Americas with colonists
entries.notes: The European plum is itself an ancient hybrid; prunes are dried European plums.

entries.name: Cherry (sweet)
entries.spread: Anatolia and Greece, then Rome (Lucullus, 74 BCE); Americas with colonists
needs: calm dry weather at harvest (rain splits fruit)
entries.notes: Very fast from blossom to fruit. Sour cherry (P. cerasus) is the pie and preserve cherry.

entries.name: Apricot

domesticated.where: China (primary origin), spread via Central Asia, Armenia and Persia

entries.spread: China to Central Asia and Persia (hence 'armeniaca'), Mediterranean, Americas after 1500; Hunza valley fame
entries.notes: Blooms notoriously early, so late frost regularly wipes out crops in cool climates.

entries.name: Fig

domesticated.where: Fertile Crescent (Gilgal I site, parthenocarpic figs)

entries.spread: the oldest known cultivated plant; Mediterranean into Rome; Americas after 1500; China Han dynasty
entries.notes: Possibly the first plant ever domesticated, ~9400 BCE, before grain. Fresh figs spoil in days; dried figs travel.

entries.name: Pomegranate
entries.spread: Persia and India across the Silk Road; entrenched in the Mediterranean; Americas with Spanish settlers
entries.notes: Symbol of fertility and abundance across the Mediterranean and Near East. Splits open when over-ripe.

entries.name: Date palm
entries.spread: Mesopotamia to the Indus valley, Arabia and North Africa; Americas (California, Arizona) after 1900; Canary and date islands
entries.notes: The anchor crop of the desert oasis; a palm can fruit for a century. Baghdad was built on date wealth.

entries.name: Olive
entries.spread: Mediterranean basin since antiquity; Americas with the Spanish after 1500 (California, Peru, Argentina)
entries.notes: Millennia-old orchards still crop; the foundation of Mediterranean cooking and trade. Fruit must be cured or pressed.

entries.name: Garden strawberry

domesticated.where: France (Versailles; accidental hybrid of Chilean and Virginian strawberries, Frézier, 1714)

entries.spread: every temperate region; California, Spain, China dominate production
entries.notes: A deliberate 18th-century hybrid; the wild strawberries it replaced were tiny but intensely flavoured.

entries.name: Watermelon
entries.spread: Egypt and the Mediterranean; India, China; Americas with the slave trade and colonists; China is now the top grower
entries.notes: Ancient Egyptian paintings show watermelons; black-seeded 'desert melons' still survive wild in Libya.

entries.name: Avocado
entries.spread: Mexico and Central America with Spanish colonists; California commercial crop from the 1880s; global tropics today
entries.notes: Large seeds once dispersed by giant ground sloths — extinct, the tree waits for planting and hands.

entries.name: Papaya
entries.spread: Mesoamerica to the Caribbean, Europe after 1492; world tropics; India now grows the most
entries.notes: Fruits on a tall cane-like stem in about a year from seed; pawpaw in Australia.

entries.name: Pineapple
entries.spread: tropical America to the Caribbean and Europe after 1492 (a sensation in courts); Hawaii, the Philippines, Thailand, Costa Rica
entries.notes: A bromeliad: one pineapple per rosette. A single fruit took 2+ years to grow at a European stove-house.

entries.name: Lemon
entries.wild_ancestor: Citrus x limon (citron x bitter orange hybrid)
entries.spread: India and the Middle East, Mediterranean by antiquity, Europe in the Middle Ages, Americas after 1492; Sicily and Amalfi famous
entries.notes: The sailor's cure for scurvy; citrus fleets ended it in the Royal Navy in the 18th century.

entries.name: Grapefruit
entries.wild_ancestor: natural hybrid of pomelo (Citrus maxima) x sweet orange
entries.spread: Barbados ~1750; Jamaica; Florida by the 1820s; Texas, Arizona, elsewhere in the subtropics
entries.notes: A fruit literally invented by nature in the 18th century; named for clusters ripening like grapes. Interacts with many medicines.

entries.name: Kiwifruit

domesticated.where: wild in the Yangtze valley, selected in New Zealand

entries.spread: China to New Zealand in 1904; renamed 'kiwi' in 1959 for export; Italy, New Zealand, China grow the most; Iran and Greece rising
entries.notes: A 20th-century success story: wild Chinese gooseberry, rebranded for export; the old Chinese name was 'yang tao'.

entries.name: Highbush blueberry

domesticated.where: United States (Elizabeth White and Frederick Coville, New Jersey/North Carolina)

entries.spread: North America after 1906; commercial from 1916; now grown across Europe and Asia
entries.notes: Domesticated only in the 20th century; one of very few crops bred almost entirely in modern times.

entries.name: Cranberry

domesticated.where: United States (first cultivated bogs, Henry Hall, Dennis, Massachusetts)

entries.spread: native to Atlantic and Gulf coastal bogs; New England and Wisconsin dominate; Chile, France, elsewhere
entries.notes: Harvested by flooding the bog; berries bounce when ripe — the old jump-test.

entries.name: Muskmelon (cantaloupe and honeydew)

domesticated.where: India or Africa (centre of origin debated)

entries.spread: Asia and Africa; Mediterranean by antiquity (Armenian muskmelons); the name 'cantaloupe' from the Italian town of Cantalupo, 15th century; global
entries.notes: One species, countless types: cantaloupe, honeydew, Persian, Charentais, hami.

entries.name: Guava
entries.spread: tropical America; by the 1550s in the Spanish Caribbean, Philippines; now dominant in India, SE Asia and Brazil
entries.notes: Softer forms are eaten fresh; firm pink ones are for pastes (goiabada, guayaba).

entries.name: Coconut palm
entries.wild_ancestor: coconut palms are not traceable to a single wild ancestor

domesticated.where: centre of domestication debated (Southeast Asia and/or Indian Ocean); spread by Austronesian seafarers, then by Indian Ocean trade

entries.spread: Pacific and Indian Ocean coasts via Austronesian and Arab sailors; Americas (Caribbean, Brazil, Pacific coast) after 1492/1500s; now in all warm coasts
entries.notes: The 'tree of life': water, flesh, oil, fibre, timber and leaves. A mature palm fruits continuously, ~50-80 nuts a year.

entries.name: Japanese persimmon
entries.spread: China to Korea and Japan in antiquity; California and worldwide in the 19th-20th century
entries.notes: Orange beacons of autumn; astringent types (hachiya) must be jelly-soft before eating, non-astringent (fuyu) can be eaten firm.

entries.name: Lychee
entries.spread: southern China and Vietnam; India, Madagascar, South Africa, Mauritius in the 18th-19th century; now 20+ countries
entries.notes: Han emperors allegedly built horse relays to rush fresh lychees to court; only weeks of fruit a year.

entries.name: Quince
entries.spread: Caucasus and Persia to the Mediterranean; known to the Greeks and Romans (the 'golden apple' of myth?); Asia minor; sparse today
entries.notes: Rock-hard and astringent raw; transforms into jelly, paste (membrillo) and perfumes.

entries.name: Breadfruit
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Artocarpus camansi (likely; Artocarpus altilis is a sterile cultigen)
entries.spread: New Guinea and island SE Asia; Polynesia and Micronesia by ancient voyagers; Captain Bligh's Bounty (1789) carried it to Jamaica; today across the wet tropics
entries.notes: Starchy, seedless, huge; one big tree can feed a household for generations. A staple of the Pacific.

entries.name: Durian
entries.spread: Malaysia and Indonesia; Thailand dominates modern exports; niche elsewhere ('forbidden' in hotels and transit)
entries.notes: 'The king of fruits': custard flesh inside a thorn-husked green shell, famous for its polarizing smell (banned on some transport).

entries.name: Dragon fruit (pitaya)
entries.spread: pre-Columbian Central America; China and Vietnam made it a major modern crop from the 1980s-90s; now across the warm dry tropics
entries.notes: A climbing night-flowering cactus; fruits glow magenta. Night-blooming, bat- and moth-pollinated.

entries.name: Passion fruit
entries.spread: Brazil to Paraguay; to Europe in the early 1600s; Australia, Africa, Asia; South Africa a major grower
entries.notes: Spanish missionaries saw the flower's parts as symbols of the Passion; the fruit is balled with edible seeds.

entries.name: Almond
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Prunus dulcis var. amara (bitter almond)
entries.spread: Fertile Crescent to the Mediterranean; California now grows the large majority of the world crop
entries.notes: Bitter wild almonds carry cyanide; the sweet mutation was the domestication event. Bitter almond oil is a flavouring.

entries.name: Pistachio
entries.spread: Central Asia and Persia; long cultivated in Iran (a world leader); California dominates modern production
entries.notes: One of the oldest nut crops; a desert-edge tree with cork-like bark and a waxy bloom.

entries.name: Persian walnut
entries.spread: Central Asia to Persia (hence 'Persian walnut'), Greece and Rome; California, Chile and China dominate today
entries.notes: The standard culinary walnut; the wrinkled shell hides a two-lobed brain-like kernel — walnuts were folk medicine for headaches.

entries.name: Hazelnut (filbert)
entries.spread: northern Europe and Anatolia since the Stone Age; Turkey grows the plurality of the world crop; Oregon, Italy, Azerbaijan
entries.notes: Possibly the oldest cultivated nut; found in Neolithic settlements. Winter-flowering, wind-pollinated, harvested in early autumn.
